title: Custody-Backed Securities Receipts: Issuance, Rights and Proof of Backing
subtitle: Depositary structure versus native securities and synthetic exposure
abstract: A receipt described as tokenized equity is meaningful only if investors know what asset backs it, which institution holds the asset, the governing holder rights, conversion ratio and enforceable exit arrangements. This report compares direct security issuance, third-party depositary receipts and synthetic exposure, then derives an independently testable custody-to-token reconciliation architecture for TSR.

evidence.heading: The legal model determines the claim
evidence.body: The January 2026 SEC staff statement explains different forms of tokenized securities and emphasizes that rights depend on the issuer and underlying legal arrangement; it is not binding law. A third-party receipt can represent an entitlement against a depositary rather than the shareholder-of-record status of the corresponding ordinary share. Token control, shareholder voting, distribution entitlements, bankruptcy priority and redemption are therefore separate disclosure and engineering requirements.

evidence.heading: Asset lifecycle extends beyond minting
evidence.body: Project Guardian's fund and tokenized collateral frameworks emphasize custody, share registers, servicing and enforcement across the instrument lifecycle. BIS and IMF research similarly warns that changing the digital record of an asset does not eliminate legal, liquidity or counterparty dependencies. Tokenization may improve coordination, but a valid asset and investor remedy must exist independently of a smart contract's balance map.

evidence.heading: A proof-of-backing must include the asset population
evidence.body: Confirming that a token contract has 10,000 units outstanding does not demonstrate that a custodian actually holds the eligible assets. Supply integrity requires an external asset inventory, legally segregated and unencumbered positions, issuer and custodian obligations, and a reconciliation of pending issuance and redemption. A successful on-chain event is only one piece of this chain of evidence.

architecture.heading: Define custody and record-of-rights boundaries
architecture.body: Identify the underlying security, legal owner, custodian account and whether the asset may be lent or rehypothecated. Distinguish shareholder of record from holder of the contractual receipt. Store signed custody attestations and the conversion ratio in a registry independent of the token interface. Each token series should reference governing terms including voting pass-through, distributions, delivery restrictions and recovery in custodian or issuer insolvency.

architecture.heading: Quantitative backing invariant
architecture.body: Let U be eligible underlying units in the designated custody pool, k receipt units supported by one underlying unit, R outstanding receipts and P pending receipts reserved for issuance. A basic check is R + P ≤ kU, after adjustment for redemptions and encumbrances. Strong assurance also verifies that every U is eligible, not pledged to another obligation, and subject to enforceable rights for receipt holders. Contract-held or authorized-but-unissued tokens require explicit treatment.

architecture.heading: Primary versus secondary transaction
architecture.body: In a primary issue an issuer or authorized participant acquires backing assets, obtains valid custody proof, authorizes receipts and allocates them against funding. In a secondary trade an existing holder transfers receipts to another and the buyer pays the seller or intermediary; it normally does not create a new capital subscription to the issuer. The custody pool can remain unchanged even though beneficial holder records and trading balances change.

architecture.heading: Exit, redemption and failure treatment
architecture.body: Specify when a holder can request cash, underlying shares or only a market sale. Redemption may involve a dealing threshold, settlement cut-off, market closure or foreign jurisdiction's transfer procedures. Freeze new issue when backing is insufficient, reconcile every authorized cancellation, and preserve legally enforceable entitlements during failed token transfers or network outages. Burning receipt units before economic redemption is final can create an unrecoverable mismatch.

case.title: Synthetic fractional equity: 1,000 shares supporting 10,000 receipts
case.setup: Assume a depositary acquires 1,000 eligible ordinary shares and defines 10 receipt units as the economic entitlement corresponding to one share. The numbers illustrate a proposed contract and do not establish any real instrument's legal rights.
rows: 10 receipts per underlying share; full backing
40 share-equivalents transfer; no additional share purchase
Disposition or cash consideration for 100 shares documented
case.formula: Backing capacity = eligible shares × 10. Before redemption 1,000 × 10 = 10,000 receipts. After 1,000 eligible receipts are redeemed and backing is proportionately released, 9,000 ÷ 10 = 900 equivalent shares.
case.interpretation: A wallet unit may convey fractional economic rights without giving the holder direct registered share ownership. The contract and evidence must say which.

risks: Missing underlying
Receipts exist but shares are not held in the designated protected account.
Independent custody confirmations and issuance gate.
Insolvency ambiguity
Holder's recovery claim against issuer, depositary and custodian is undocumented.
Legal opinion, segregation evidence, priority and claims waterfall.
Exit mismatch
Issuer promises physical delivery but fractional or nonresident holders cannot receive underlying shares.
Define cash-in-lieu, thresholds, eligibility and fees.
tests: Test issuance, three secondary trades and a redemption with an independent custodian feed; no token unit may be unbacked.
Compare voting, dividends, insolvency and physical-redemption rights in issuer-native, receipt and synthetic securities.
Deliberately remove 25 underlying shares without decreasing receipt supply and require an immediate deficit alert.
conclusion: Custody-backed tokenization must make rights, backing, allocation and redemption demonstrably consistent across separate institutions. TSR should treat the custody-to-receipt reconciliation as a foundational control—not an optional administrative report.

title: Corporate Actions and Fractional Securities: Entitlement and Servicing
subtitle: Record dates, dividends, splits, cash-in-lieu and the beneficial ownership register
abstract: Fractional token units do not eliminate corporate action administration. Dividends, splits, votes, spin-offs, tender offers and withholding each require accurate holder snapshots and custody-to-issuer reconciliation. A depositary receipt holder may have proportionate economic interests without standing as registered shareholder. This report specifies how to allocate rights without duplicating or silently extinguishing them.

evidence.heading: Asset servicing is integral to tokenized capital markets
evidence.body: Project Guardian's Operationalising Tokenised Funds framework addresses share-register models, fund operations and asset servicing rather than simply token transfer. IMF research evaluates tokenization across origination, trading, post-trade and administration. The implication is that an asset token without complete servicing and exception handling is an incomplete financial instrument.

evidence.heading: Holder status determines entitlements
evidence.body: The SEC's 2026 nonbinding staff statement distinguishes direct tokenized securities and third-party arrangements. A receipt holder's pass-through rights depend on the depositary contract, while voting and dividends flow through legally recognized chain-of-title and record-date rules. A token transfer block timestamp alone may not determine the economic holder during unsettled trades or custody record corrections.

evidence.heading: Market price does not settle distribution rights
evidence.body: A token may trade when its reference exchange is closed, with spot prices reflecting order-book liquidity and other risks. That trading price does not allocate dividends or correct a split, and it cannot resolve the custodian's final cash receipts. The FSB discusses vulnerabilities from asynchronous or fragmented token markets. A receipt platform must distinguish indicative market prices from the legally defined entitlement schedule.

architecture.heading: Corporate action event taxonomy
architecture.body: Track notification, confirmation, ex-date, record date, effective date, payment date and any election deadline as separate events, each linked to the official instrument identifier and trusted source. Create an immutable versioned event and record approved corrections. The token register may need a freeze, lock or post-event adjustment, but retroactive changes require formal authority.

architecture.heading: Beneficial owner and entitlement snapshot
architecture.body: Determine eligible holders by the legally applicable record-date rules, not merely by a current wallet query. Disputes can arise from pending settlement, omnibus custody, lending, wrapped tokens or transfers in flight. The entitlement calculation should use a frozen, independently reconstructible population and a prescribed treatment of encumbered or unsettled interests.

architecture.heading: Gross-to-net dividend accounting
architecture.body: Let gross distribution G be the custodian's amount received; let W denote legally required withholding, F fees and R rounding or unclaimed liabilities. Amount available to be paid to holders equals G − W − F − R, with unpaid amounts preserved as recognized liabilities rather than disappearing as dust. Each investor entitlement must reconcile to a payable and settlement voucher.

architecture.heading: Stock splits and rights conversions
architecture.body: A split alters underlying share count and the entitlement conversion ratio or receipt supply in a contractually specified way; it should not by itself create economic wealth. Spin-offs and mergers may replace the underlying identifier, create cash consideration or impose holder elections. The issuer must record those changes independently and verify receipt supply after the action before reopening transfer.

case.title: Synthetic dividend, withholding and split
case.setup: A depositary holds 500 shares supporting 5,000 receipts. The share issuer declares a USD 2.00 dividend. For illustration assume a uniform 15% withholding rate and zero fees; actual tax depends on the instrument, jurisdiction and holder.
rows: Legal rate and investor residency need verification
At 10 receipts/share, supply 5,000 → 7,500 if terms prescribe fixed ratio
case.formula: 1,000 gross = 150 withholding + 850 net. Net/receipt = 850 / 5,000 = 0.17. A 3:2 split changes share units, not mechanically the holder's economic wealth.
case.interpretation: The split scenario assumes the receipt ratio remains fixed and the issuer is contractually authorized to adjust the supply; the alternative is adjusting the ratio and leaving receipts unchanged.

risks: Duplicate distribution
Custodied underlying and wrapped token each appear eligible for the same income.
Canonical entitlement register and prevention of double allocation.
Snapshot race
Secondary transfer settles after a block snapshot but before legal record-date cut-off.
Define authoritative date/time and unresolved transfers.
Rounding loss
Small payouts are silently rounded to zero.
Rounding liability and cumulative reconciliation.
tests: Simulate a dividend with pledged, frozen, wrapped and unsettled receipts; compute one economically valid recipient per unit.
Run split, reverse split, rights offer and cash-in-lieu, checking custody-versus-receipt ratio and journal balances.
Model distribution failure in one payment rail without paying the same holder twice.
conclusion: Fractional access is not a complete product unless corporate-action entitlements can be administered and independently verified. TSR should model servicing, withholding and record-date transformations as first-class financial state changes.

title: Bond, Fund and Collateral Tokenization: Three Different Lifecycles
subtitle: Debt service, NAV issuance and encumbered assets on shared infrastructure
abstract: Tokenized bonds, fund interests and pledged collateral are sometimes grouped as homogeneous RWA tokens. They are not homogeneous financial claims. Bond obligations have interest and maturity schedules; fund shares have NAV and dealing rules; collateral entails priority, valuation, substitution and enforcement. This report distinguishes their rights models and develops a common event-and-assurance infrastructure.

evidence.heading: Bond tokenization does not erase debt-service obligations
evidence.body: The BIS 2025 government-bond tokenisation bulletin assesses opportunities and continuing infrastructure constraints. A bond token remains a claim against an issuer whose principal, coupon, ranking, covenants and remedy depend on enforceable documentation. Token issuance speed does not guarantee improved liquidity or automatic performance of the issuer's obligations.

evidence.heading: Fund lifecycle has transfer-agent and NAV dependencies
evidence.body: Project Guardian's asset-management materials examine fund subscriptions, redemptions, registers and servicing. Investors generally acquire and redeem fund units according to fund terms and NAV calculations rather than continuous independently executable token pricing. A receipt token or fund token should make dealing dates, price uncertainty and fund-administrator corrections explicit.

evidence.heading: Collateral is a security interest, not necessarily fresh issuer capital
evidence.body: The secured party may obtain an enforceable pledge while the original owner retains relevant economic exposure. An electronic lock can restrict transfers but does not alone establish lien perfection, priority, eligibility or recovery rights. The FSB's tokenisation-risk analysis and BIS settlement prototypes show why cross-institution coordination is necessary when collateral and payment obligations are represented in different systems.

architecture.heading: Three separate authoritative ledgers
architecture.body: A bond registry records face principal, series, holder identity, coupon accrual and maturity. A fund's transfer agent records shares, subscription/redemption status, class rights and NAV. A collateral register captures pledgor, secured party, asset, lien, haircut, release and enforcement. The token representation can share technical infrastructure while preserving these business-state distinctions and separate controls.

architecture.heading: Money and asset movements have different meaning
architecture.body: Primary bond placement funds the issuer; a tokenized fund subscription increases fund assets and share supply; a collateral pledge usually changes asset availability and priority without increasing the underlying security issuer's capital. Secondary trades generally pay the holder selling an existing instrument. Financial reports should not consolidate all four as gross capital formation.

architecture.heading: Calculation and settlement layers
architecture.body: Bond coupon = contractual principal × coupon rate × period fraction. A fund investor's redeemed cash depends on valid unit balance, dealing NAV and fees. Eligible collateral value depends on mark-to-market, haircut and credit policy. DvP may exchange a bond against money; collateral substitution requires secured party acceptance before old pledged assets are released. One generic 'token transfer' function cannot establish those conditions.

architecture.heading: Distinguish demonstration from adoption
architecture.body: BIS and Project Guardian projects illustrate technical patterns, not uniform market readiness. Compare cost, legal uncertainty, operational roles, on-chain privacy, dispute resolution and liquidity supply against conventional systems. Where tokenization may reduce reconciliation friction, measure end-to-end operations rather than individual blockchain throughput.

case.title: Worked bond coupon and pledged position
case.setup: Hypothetical bond principal USD 2 million, 4% annual coupon paid quarterly. A holder pledges USD 500,000 face value as collateral, with an illustrative 10% haircut and unchanged assumed market price.
rows: Debt and registered creditor positions created
Restricted ownership/pledge record; bond supply unchanged
Assumed eligible collateral value, not face-value guarantee
No new issuance, no bond cancellation
case.formula: Quarterly contractual coupon = 2,000,000 × 4% ÷ 4 = $20,000. Haircut-adjusted collateral = 500,000 × (1 − 10%) = $450,000 under the stated assumptions.
case.interpretation: An issuer's debt, a holder's collateral encumbrance and a coupon payment are separate economic events despite common digital interfaces.

risks: Wrong bond liability
Token balances ignore missed coupon or principal default status.
Paying-agent reconciliation and default event handling.
Fund price mismatch
Transfers and redemptions offered at continuous spot price although fund NAV is periodic.
Clear subscription/redemption cut-off rules and NAV disclosure.
Multiple liens
Same token is pledged to several independent secured parties.
Shared encumbrance identifiers, enforceable priority and independent monitoring.
tests: Implement bond coupon, fund redemption and collateral substitution using a common evidence schema but three financial state machines.
Simulate collateral value falling below margin threshold and test secure substitution and enforcement authorization.
Report capital formation, secondary trading and collateral reuse as separate metrics.
conclusion: RWA token systems need instrument-specific rights engines even when using reusable token and settlement infrastructure. The experimental priority is proving consistency among the asset, the obligation, the registry, the payment and the holder's enforceable rights.
